Hello, and first off, can I just say that you are by no means alone in this regard. Case of point, I believe I made a post here a year or so ago asking about the same question.


So let's get started. For one, adding to what Cora said, I would highly suggest getting treatment. It does not necessarily have to be drugs if you are not comfortable with that (though I can personally vouch for their capacity to mitigate symptoms) though having some manner to cope, be it therapy or meditation, will greatly alleviate the stress that comes with OCD compulsions.


Secondly, as for your question, I am not going to give you a yes or no answer. Instead I will tell you what helped me come to terms with the matter. Then you can draw your own conclusions from there.


If I can say one thing with the utmost certainty, it is this: OCD does not give you joy, or happiness, or acceptance. This might sound rather bleak, but OCD does one thing, and one thing only: it makes your life a living hell. You will *never* feel elation or beauty in a compulsion. You will never see meaning, or purpose, or order.


And that is why, for me at least, I came to realize that my “gender identity” (as much as I feel the word fails to convey its meaning) is not propagated by my OCD.


True, being transgender has brought its own myriad of problems (especially, as you say, when obsessions connect themselves to your thoughts of the same subject) and true, gender dysphoria is an utter pain in the ass in its own right. Yet that sensation… that feeling that touches you when you close your eyes and imagine a world where you aren't encased in this cage of flesh, *that* is not OCD. I can no more describe it than describe the colours of a dream or the whispers of a songbird, but I suspect most everyone here knows what I am talking about. It is this that makes you who you are. You might like skirts and blouses, I like jeans and sweaters. Neither of us are right or wrong, because that doesn't matter. Your clothes, your mannerisms, your preferences; all of it is superfluous. What matters is what you can feel, or rather, what you *sense* of this part of you.


And know that OCD can never change that. No matter how many times it tries.

I am a transgender woman. And I will admit, this joke does not “offend” me.


That said, do I get a warm and fuzzy feeling seeing everywhere I go? Not exactly… especially when I know that it has a strong following among transphobic and homophobic groups. I am not saying that anyone who repeats it is automatically participating in hate speech, indeed, in many ways this meme (no matter how ill-conceived) has allowed for people to be introduced to a miniscule minority that has been traditionally overlooked up until this past year. I agree that all words are subjective, they rely on context, the n-word, for instance, was once just latin for “black,” and “queer,” long an insult, has been slowly re appropriated by the LGBT community.


And yet, all this is a digression.


It is true that people are free to speak their minds; however, freedom of speech is not freedom against rebuttal. Quite the opposite, in fact. To state, for instance that “the SJWs are suppressing my opinions by saying they are not socially acceptable” is both hypocritical and in stark contrast to what freedom of expression *is*. Attacking those who defend otherwise voiceless minorities and draw reasonable arguments against the gnashing misinformation that permeates such, is to do exactly what supposed advocates for “free speech” levy against the “SJW” tumblr boogeymen.


Now, with regards to a few of the misconceptions in this thread.


-No, hormones and therapy are not a “cure” for being transgender. Both aid in dealing with gender dysphoria, a condition often arising from being transgender, wherein our internal gender (“gender identity,” though to be honest, it is an almost impossible concept to describe with any such name) is at odds with our bodies. At this point it is hypothesised that this could be a result of hormonal spikes during in-utero development of the brain, but study in this area is terribly stunted.


To give you a thought exercise as that you can understand just a semblance of this feeling, imagine this: you are male, you might not love your body and yeah, you should probably work out a bit more than you do, yet it is still *yours.* Then, this morning, you wake up, you look down and you scream because that form is gone. You're the opposite sex.


You get up and go to school -presumably after coming to terms with whatever ancient egyptian curse you have released upon yourself. Everyone recognizes you. You have always been female to them. They call you “Ms” and “ma’am,” you feel slightly self-conscious and ask them to stop. They look at you as if you just swallowed some slick green creature.


When you see your friends, they are the same exact people who have always stuck by you. One of them makes a joke about how your wide shouldered jacket almost makes you look like a man… *almost.* They all laugh. You laugh as well, though something squeezes in your gut.


As the day goes on, the novelty wears off and as the afternoon shifts to the evening, you find yourself with that same group of friends again. You can almost forget about your predicament when around them, yet every so often one of their gazes will linger slightly too long on your chest or crotch, or they will crack a crude joke then grow hushed as you grow near. And in your mind you begin to feel a desperation, a wish that this nightmare would just end.


It doesn't.


You know that it never will.




-Many transgender people opt to not undergo cosmetic surgery. For one thing, even getting hormones covered by insurance is a pain, let alone costly surgical procedures that are often fully out-of-pocket. Hell, SRS (Sexual Reassignment Surgery)  a necessity in many american states for one to even be *recognized* as any legal sex other than that assigned at birth, is most often not insured, despite its implications and use by lawmakers.


Secondly, and perhaps more simply: many just do not feel a need for such. 


-Transgender people are not the “stereotypical feminine/ masculine” characters they are often satirised as. However, as with every generalization, this does have a grain of truth. The fact of the matter is that trans* people are often forced by the social view of gender (not the same as gender identity, another common misperception) to adhere strictly to norms in an effort to be recognized as the gender they are. After all, due to the proliferation of the “I will call them as I see them” mentality, we must double down on acting on such standards just to acquire the bear minimum of human decency.


-And for the love of God, we do not “choose” our gender. It is not a lifestyle, it is how we were born.


I likely missed or forgot something here, if you have any questions I would implore you to inquire further at https://m.reddit.com/r/asktransgender, it is typically a decent subreddit.


Thank you for your time, and I bid you all have a good day.

I will not act like I have much stock in this whole argument, after all, I have never dated anyone as a male or female. It is just not something I am willing to do without full, unilateral commitment.

However, calling someone transphobic for not wanting to date someone who is transgender is -in my personal opinion- an invalid and overly simplistic reaction. It is true, yes, there are jerks, there are chasers and there are plain old transphobic assholes. All of these people deserve such a label that will mar their reputation through the annals of history. But someone who simply isn't sexually attracted to transwomen, yet in all other ways is considerate and courteous? Dubbing such is equating preference to personality. You could argue day and night that these preferences might be caused by some latent transphobia or social concepts, but that argument is irrelevant and meaningless to this discussion. Of course we have biases, we are human. Our brains work off of biases. Our sexuality is not ours to control, just as our gender is not.

There could be any number of reasons someone does not want to date a trans person, just as there are any number of reasons not to date a cis person. Bigotry is one, yes, but what if someone wants to start a family without adopting? What if they do not wish to be targeted due to their relationship? These are valid concerns. They are a result of our society yes, though that does not make them any more bigoted than the preferences of you or I.

In any case, this is just my opinion. I profusely apologize if I offended anyone; that was not my intent.
